what: ONE Gas distributes natural gas. It is the regulated utility delivering gas to homes and businesses in Oklahoma, Kansas and Texas, operating the pipelines and meters that bring gas to about two and a half million customers.
customers: Households and businesses in Oklahoma, Kansas and Texas heating with natural gas, with rates set by each state’s regulator.
money: Gas delivery to residential, commercial and industrial customers across three states.
moat: A regulated gas distribution utility holds a legal monopoly in its service territory, with rates set to allow a return on the capital invested in the network. Nobody else may deliver gas to those customers, the pipes cannot be duplicated, and replacing ageing pipe earns a regulated return — which makes earnings growth predictable if the regulators are reasonable.
risks: Free cash flow was about negative $159.5M, because the utility is investing heavily in pipe replacement.
Debt of $2.6B against $10.6M of cash is heavy, which is normal for a utility but makes it sensitive to interest rates.
Revenue swings with gas prices passing through to customers, from $2.6B in 2022 to $2.1B in 2024, which obscures the underlying business.
Long-term electrification of home heating reduces gas demand, which is a structural question for every gas distributor.
Nine analysts average an $86.61 target, only 7% above the current price.
opportunities: A regulated monopoly across three states produces predictable, inflation-adjusted revenue.
The shares trade at about 17.2 times earnings and 9.8 times EV/EBITDA, reasonable for a regulated utility.
Pipe replacement programmes earn a regulated return on the capital spent, which grows earnings reliably.
Last year’s net margin was 10.9%, solid for a gas distributor.
Oklahoma, Kansas and Texas are relatively constructive regulatory jurisdictions and growing population centres.
watch: Rate base growth and rate case outcomes. A regulated utility earns the allowed return on invested capital, so those two things determine almost all of the earnings.
view: ONE Gas is about as simple as a listed company gets: it owns the pipes that deliver natural gas to two and a half million homes and businesses in Oklahoma, Kansas and Texas, nobody else may deliver gas to them, and a regulator sets what it may charge. Earnings grow when the invested capital in the network grows. So a pipe replacement programme is not a cost — it is the mechanism by which the company grows, because the regulator allows a return on the money spent.

That makes the negative free cash flow of $159 million a feature rather than a warning. The company is spending more than it earns on network investment, which increases the rate base on which it is paid. The same applies to the $2.6 billion of debt: utilities finance long-lived assets with long-dated debt, and the regulator’s allowed return is set with that structure in mind. Rising interest rates do hurt, because the cost of new debt rises faster than rate cases can adjust.

The revenue line should be ignored entirely. It went from $2.6 billion to $2.1 billion and back to $2.4 billion, which reflects the price of gas passing through to customers rather than anything about the business — a utility that buys gas cheaply and passes the saving on reports lower revenue and identical earnings. Rate base and allowed return are the only figures that describe this company.

The long-dated structural question is electrification: climate policy points toward heating buildings with electricity rather than gas, and over decades that reduces the demand for gas distribution. It is slow, politically contested in these particular states, and partly offset by the fact that somebody must maintain the network for as long as anyone uses it. At 17.2 times earnings with nine analysts seeing 7% of upside, this is fairly priced for what it is: a dependable regulated earner with a very long-dated headwind.
bull: Pipe replacement keeps growing the rate base at an allowed return in constructive jurisdictions, producing dependable low-risk earnings growth and a reliable dividend.
bear: Rates stay high against $2.6 billion of debt, regulators push back on recovery, and heating electrification slowly erodes the customer base.
